The issue before the court is the meaning and implementation of the judicial rule of statutory strict construction. That was the basis the trial judge used to justify his decision to dissolve the writs of garnishment in this case. It appears to me, however, that the rule of strict construction is often invoked or cited in case law, but without a very thorough analysis of what is actually meant and how the concept is to be applied in differing fact situations. So I am advocating that the court adopt an interpretation of strict construction that is not absolute and unbending, but that takes into account differing circumstances in particular cases. And when that version of the rule is applied to this particular case, requires the reversal of the trial judge's decisions in dismissing the writs or dissolving the writs. So my proposal can be summed up as basically as follows, is that if a particular statute that mandates an action by a party states that, and states that the rule and states a time limit, for instance, within which that action is to be taken. And if the statute states that if that action is not done within the stated time, then there's a stated consequence. Then the court is duty bound to follow the dictates of the legislature and to honor the statutory language as written. If on the other hand, if the statute is silent as to a consequence of a failure to do something that's otherwise required, then obviously the legislature has not expressed its intent as to what the consequence should be. And by default, the decision's left to the trial court to decide what the remedy or what the consequence should be. And I believe that in making that decision, the trial court should take into account the individual particular circumstances surrounding that particular breach of the statute.
